exam: A 10‑month‑old child presents with lethargy and a MUAC of 10.5 cm. What is the next step? — Start therapeutic feeding (RUTF) and investigate for infection (malaria, diarrhoea).
You measure a MUAC of 11.2 cm in a 3‑year‑old with a history of diarrhoea. How do you classify the child? — Moderately malnourished (yellow zone).
A child with a MUAC of 9.8 cm is admitted. Which drug should be avoided due to risk of haemolysis? — Primaquine (in G6PD deficiency).
You are in a rural clinic with no scale. How do you assess chronic malnutrition? — Use MUAC and height‑for‑age; refer if MUAC <12.5 cm or height‑for‑age Z‑score <−2.
A child with severe malnutrition is receiving RUTF. What is the most common complication to monitor? — Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphatemia).
You suspect HIV in a child with low MUAC. Which test is most feasible in a low‑resource setting? — Rapid HIV antibody test.
A child with a MUAC of 12.0 cm has a large head relative to body. What does this suggest? — Marasmus (acute protein‑energy wasting).
You have a child with oedema and a MUAC of 13.0 cm. Why might this be misleading? — Oedema inflates MUAC, masking true nutritional status.
ai.title: Mid Upper Arm Circumference
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: MUAC is a simple, bedside tool to assess acute malnutrition in children over six months. It predicts mortality risk and guides therapeutic feeding and referral. In low‑resource settings it is the primary screening method.

b: Normal MUAC: ≥12.5 cm in children 6–59 months; ≥13.5 cm in children 5–12 years; ≥24 cm in pregnant women
sections.p: Mid‑Upper Arm Circumference is the girth of the arm measured at the midpoint between the acromion and olecranon. It is taken with a non‑stretchable tape, with the child relaxed and the arm at the side.

b: Severely malnourished: <11.0 cm (red) – >30 % mortality in 6 months
sections.p: MUAC thresholds classify nutritional status and mortality risk. The WHO colour‑coded tape simplifies interpretation.

Children with low MUAC often appear thin, with visible ribs and a ‘large head’ relative to body. They may have stunted growth, delayed milestones, and increased susceptibility to infections.
MUAC is a screening tool; further workup depends on clinical context. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and simple anthropometry guide management.
Severe MUAC (<11 cm) signals imminent danger. Immediate action is required to prevent mortality.

b: Refer to nutrition centre if MUAC <11 cm or not improving
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide therapeutic feeding and supportive care. In low‑resource settings, ready‑to‑use therapeutic foods (RUTF) are the mainstay.

sections.p: Regular MUAC monitoring identifies recovery or relapse. Prevention focuses on food security, infection control, and maternal nutrition.

b: Mid‑arm skinfold thickness – measures fat, not overall nutrition
sections.p: MUAC is distinct from mid‑arm skinfold thickness, which measures subcutaneous fat. Skinfold is not used for acute malnutrition screening.

b: Short stature may lower MUAC despite adequate nutrition
sections.p: MUAC can be falsely normal in children with oedema or short stature. In oedematous children, MUAC may overestimate nutritional status.
